# Summary of Information about Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer born in Mount Vernon, New York. Early in her career, she worked at IBM Research starting in 1964 on the Advanced Computing Systems project, where she contributed to the invention of multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, an innovation foundational to superscalar processor design. After beginning a gender transition in 1967 and completing it in 1968, Conway was fired by IBM but later restarted her career stealthily, working as a contract programmer, digital system designer, and computer architect at notable companies including Memorex and Xerox PARC.
At Xerox PARC, Conway led the "LSI Systems" group and co-founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology. She collaborated with Ivan Sutherland and Carver Mead to develop the groundbreaking Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology, significantly simplifying chip design with dimensionless, scalable design rules and pioneering internet-based rapid prototyping infrastructure institutionalized as MOSIS. This methodology spurred massive industry innovation, the growth of electronic design automation, and numerous technology startups. In 1978, Conway taught a seminal VLSI design course at MIT, validating the new design methods and textbook. She later worked at DARPA, contributing to the Strategic Computing Initiative, and then served as professor and associate dean at the University of Michigan until retiring in 1998.
Lynn Conway was also a transgender rights activist, publicly sharing her story starting in the late 1990s, advocating for transgender inclusion and protections in technology fields and beyond. Her courage and scientific contributions have been recognized through numerous awards including the IEEE Fellow distinction, membership in the National Academy of Engineering, the IEEE Computer Society Computer Pioneer Award, and the IBM Lifetime Achievement Award. After decades of pioneering work largely unrecognized due to her gender transition, her impact on computer science, chip design, and technology innovation is widely acknowledged, along with her advocacy for equal opportunity for transgender individuals in STEM. Conway passed away at her home in 2024 at age 86.
